title: Microsoft exec called AI scraping the “largest theft of labor in human history”
gist: Unsealed internal documents in the NYT-led copyright lawsuit reveal Microsoft and OpenAI insiders privately called news scraping for AI training a 'doom loop' and 'astonishing theft,' with Microsoft's own data showing 83-94% click-through declines for some news plaintiffs, while news organizations argue this internal evidence of anticipated harm should defeat the companies' fair-use defense at trial.

insights.claim: Microsoft Director of Applied Science Brent Hecht repeatedly warned internally that scraping news content for AI training was 'an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions,' calling it perhaps the 'largest theft of labor in human history,' and separately said the practice made 'a complete mockery of the idea of fair use.'
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: A senior Microsoft scientist's own words undercutting the company's fair-use legal defense is a significant piece of internal evidence that could sway the pending summary judgment ruling and eventual trial outcome against Microsoft and OpenAI.
insights.quote: an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions
insights.locator: Microsoft Director of Applied Science Brent Hecht repeatedly warned

insights.claim: OpenAI ChatGPT head Nick Turley wrote internally that publishers would face an 'existential threat' from commercial AI products trained on news content that could substitute for news providers, and later described chatbots as 'largely substitutive, period,' predicting they would become more substitutive as they improve.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: A senior OpenAI executive's internal prediction that chatbots will become increasingly substitutive for news is a forward-looking admission that strengthens the plaintiffs' substitution argument and signals continued pressure on news publisher traffic/revenue.
insights.locator: He also seemingly suggested that the doom loop was already in motion

insights.claim: A Microsoft internal document described a 'doom loop' in which AI scraping of news content would 'hurt the performance of our models and the entire web at the same time,' acknowledging the end-product (LLMs) threatens the economic foundations of its own essential content suppliers.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Microsoft's own internal recognition of a self-destructive feedback loop between AI products and content supply is a structural long-term risk to LLM training-data quality across the industry, not just a legal liability.
insights.quote: It is highly unusual that an end-product threatens the economic foundations of its essential suppliers, but that is the situation we have created for our LLM business with respect to its ‘content supply chain,’
insights.locator: One Microsoft document even described a “doom loop”

insights.claim: Hecht acknowledged internally that 'almost no one intended for content they created to be used in this fashion, nor are they compensated for its use,' regarding how news content ended up training AI models.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: An admission of non-consent and non-compensation from within Microsoft directly supports the plaintiffs' core copyright and fair-use arguments.
insights.quote: almost no one intended for content they created to be used in this fashion, nor are they compensated for its use

insights.claim: Microsoft's own internal data recorded 83-93% drops in click-through rates for some news plaintiffs and 51-94% drops for others, corroborating predictions that AI products would substitute for and divert traffic from original news sources.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Quantified click-through collapse of up to 94% is concrete, discoverable evidence of commercial harm that plaintiffs can use to demonstrate substitution and defeat a fair-use defense at trial — a bellwether metric for the broader news industry's AI-driven traffic decline.
insights.locator: Data from both firms shows that this prediction was accurate

insights.claim: An OpenAI software engineer stated internally that 'no matter how prominently we show the links, users won't click,' while Turley separately said there is 'no good reason to click' when the chatbot already provides the information directly.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Direct internal acknowledgment that link placement/prominence does not meaningfully drive click-through undercuts any argument that AI platforms are adequately directing traffic back to publishers, reinforcing the traffic-cannibalization thesis for the news industry.
insights.quote: no matter how prominently we show the links, users won’t click
insights.locator: There’s consensus on that at OpenAI

insights.claim: After ChatGPT's launch, Google quickly introduced AI Overviews, which the article says began absorbing even more traffic that previously went to news sites, extending the substitution problem beyond just Microsoft and OpenAI to the broader AI industry.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: The traffic-diversion dynamic is industry-wide, not confined to the defendants in this suit, implying any adverse fair-use ruling could have ripple effects on Google and other AI search/summary products.
insights.locator: Most notably, after ChatGPT’s launch, Google’s AI Overviews

insights.claim: News organizations found that chatbots would reproduce long excerpts of articles verbatim in response to prompts like requests for summaries, key bullet points, bias ratings, or picking any article off a site's homepage — techniques that went beyond earlier simple 'what's the next line?' probing.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Documented, reproducible methods for extracting verbatim copyrighted text from chatbots (bias-rating prompts, homepage article picks) are concrete evidence plaintiffs will use to prove infringement, and the plaintiffs are focusing their summary judgment ask specifically on outputs with extensive verbatim overlap.
insights.locator: In some cases, news organizations found that chatbots

insights.claim: When an OpenAI staffer told President Greg Brockman that a workaround ('a hack') had been found for OpenAI crawlers to bypass the New York Times paywall, Brockman replied approvingly, 'Ah, nice.'
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: A casual, approving response from OpenAI's president to a paywall-bypass hack is damaging internal evidence of knowing, sanctioned circumvention of publisher access controls, strengthening the plaintiffs' bad-faith argument.
insights.locator: when a staffer, Nick Ryder, informed President Greg Brockman

insights.claim: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella testified under oath that AI companies shouldn't violate news sites' terms of use by circumventing paywalls, while separately acknowledging chatbots have substituted for news platforms by providing information directly rather than requiring users to visit the source.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Sworn testimony from Microsoft's CEO acknowledging substitution effects is a high-value admission for plaintiffs even as Microsoft's legal team attempts to characterize it as mere 'observation' rather than a legal conclusion.
insights.quote: giving you the information right there on the website on the AI platform versus needing to go to the underlying source
insights.locator: Nadella also acknowledged that chatbots have served as substitutes

themes.theme: Data sourcing and consent violations alleged

insights.claim: News plaintiffs accuse Microsoft of violating industry norms by repurposing a dataset originally purchased for Bing search as training data for OpenAI, allegedly without consulting the news organizations that would not have consented to that reuse of their basic search-crawling permission.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Alleged repurposing of search-crawl data for LLM training without renewed consent is a specific legal theory of data misuse that, if proven, could set precedent limiting how search-indexed content can be reused for AI training industry-wide.
insights.locator: their motion accused Microsoft of violating “industry norms”

insights.claim: OpenAI allegedly obtained a New York Times dataset of 1.8 million articles from a third party bound by an agreement restricting commercial use, and OpenAI employees reportedly knew it 'would not be appropriate' to use that data to train a model but did so anyway.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: An alleged specific, named dataset (1.8 million NYT articles) used despite internal awareness of contractual restrictions is a concrete, provable instance of knowing misuse that strengthens plaintiffs' willfulness argument, which could affect damages calculations.
insights.locator: OpenAI allegedly “acted improperly” by obtaining a NYT dataset

insights.claim: News plaintiffs allege Microsoft and OpenAI built a filter that Hecht suggested could be perceived as an 'accidental cover up,' making it harder for content owners to see what was used for training, rather than addressing the substitution harms directly.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: An internally flagged 'accidental cover up' framing, rather than remediation, suggests the companies prioritized limiting legal discoverability over addressing the underlying harm — a fact pattern that could support punitive damages arguments.
insights.locator: instead of preventing the outputs, the firms tried to make it harder

insights.claim: News plaintiffs argue that if courts rule AI training on news content is not fair use, it would resolve a 'prisoners' dilemma' where individual AI companies benefit from free-riding on content even though the whole industry would be better off if everyone paid to sustain the content supply chain.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: The 'prisoners' dilemma' framing is a persuasive economic argument plaintiffs are using to argue courts must intervene because no individual AI company will unilaterally start paying for content absent a legal mandate — relevant to how any adverse ruling could force industry-wide licensing deals.
insights.quote: AI companies remain powerless to break out of this ‘doom loop,’ because, while the industry as a whole would benefit if every company paid to sustain the continued production of the creative works their technology depends on, each individual company is better off taking content for free while others pay,
insights.locator: “AI companies remain powerless to break out

insights.claim: OpenAI President Greg Brockman wrote internally that he was 'deeply motivated by the gazillions' that could be gained by commercializing OpenAI's technology, evidence plaintiffs cite as showing profit motive outweighed awareness of harm.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: A leadership-level statement of profit motivation, paired with internal harm warnings that were reportedly not acted on, is a rhetorical and evidentiary asset for plaintiffs seeking to characterize the conduct as willful rather than inadvertent.
insights.locator: their motion emphasized that Brockman wrote

insights.claim: Microsoft disclaims the significance of Hecht's internal comments, stating through a spokesperson that they 'reflect one employee's individual perspective, are not a legal analysis, and do not represent the company's views,' while news plaintiffs' counsel says the documents prove the companies knew their conduct was wrong.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: The dueling characterizations (isolated employee opinion vs. proof of knowing wrongdoing) will be a central battleground at trial over how much weight internal admissions carry against corporate liability.
insights.quote: reflect one employee’s individual perspective, are not a legal analysis, and do not represent the company’s views
insights.locator: Regarding Hecht’s comments, the spokesperson claimed
